My academic trajectory was shaped by early experiences outside traditional research settings, including environmental education at sea and applied ethnoecology studies in Iceland, the Faroe Islands, Lao PDR, and Vietnam [@whitney_survey_2012; @whitney_conservation_2014; @whitney_learning_2016; @whitney_ethnobotany_2013; @lee_government_2011]. These experiences reinforced my focus on leadership, education, decision-making under uncertainty and participatory approaches. 

During my PhD, I investigated the agrobiodiversity and ethnobotany of homegardens in Uganda, emphasizing their role in nutrition and food security [@whitney_homegardens_2017; @whitney_crop_2018; @whitney_ethnobotany_2018]. These formative experiences laid the foundation for my current research applying decision analysis to interdisciplinary challenges. I developed a Monte Carlo-based framework for evaluating intervention efficacy, integrating expert-elicited probabilistic models to quantify uncertainty in agroecological systems [@whitney_decision_2023]. I also developed tools to support research, including the ethnobotanyR package for quantitative ethnobotanical studies [@whitney_ethnobotanyr_2021]. This tool facilitated my collaborative research on cultural heritage, such as documenting medicinal teas in China [@abdusalam_documenting_2020] and the use and conservation of fig species in Myanmar [@mon_uses_2020].

The work I present in this thesis spans the six years since I completed my PhD in Agricultural Sciences at the University of Kassel in 2018. Over this period, I have held roles across institutions and projects, all linked by a focus on sustainable development and agroecology. 

After earning my PhD, I started as a consultant with the World Agroforestry Centre (ICRAF), contributing to CGIAR WLE-funded projects in Uganda, Kenya, and Burkina Faso, focusing on modeling for sustainable land use and agricultural development. I also joined the Center for Development Research (ZEF). My work included research on agricultural adaptation to climate extremes and the consequences of shifting agricultural frontiers in response to global climate dynamics [@del_barrio_climate_2020]. 

At the University of Bonn’s Institute of Crop Science and Resource Conservation (INRES), I now lead the Holistic Systems Analysis team. Our research focuses on developing modeling approaches to address system complexity, with a particular emphasis on decision-making in agroecology, agroforestry, and horticultural systems. While much of our work centers on the tropics and subtropics, we also engage in research on temperate agricultural systems. I am responsible for advancing the core methods within the research group, which includes maintaining an R package that is made available to the broader scientific community. I also continuously improve the participatory elements of our models to better engage with local stakeholders and decision-makers. I help oversee seven third-party-funded projects and I am the Principal Investigator for the project Nutrition Intervention Forecasting and Monitoring (NIFAM) funded by the German Federal Office for Agriculture and Food (BLE) (€1,260,000 2022-2026) applying decision analysis to nutrition and agricultural interventions. 

Beyond research, I contribute to teaching MSc programs such as Agricultural Sciences and Resource Management in the Tropics and Subtropics (ARTS), delivering courses on Decision Analysis, R Programming, and Modeling. Additionally, I teach interdisciplinary research and systems analysis courses through the Bonn International Graduate School for Development Research (BIGS-DR) at ZEF. I have delivered invited lectures at international institutions, including Cambridge and Goettingen, and have co-supervised graduate students across Europe and Asia. I have played a pivotal role in training PhD students at the Center for Development Research (ZEF), where I co-lead an annual introductory course in R programming as part of the Bonn International Graduate School for Development Research (BIGS-DR). In addition to this course, I contribute to doctoral-level courses on decision analysis and related topics. This teaching and mentoring work, which extends beyond my formal teaching obligations, has been instrumental in enhancing the methodological skills of PhD candidates in development research, many of whom apply these skills in third-party-funded research projects. I have introduced innovative approaches to experiential learning, my teaching philosophy emphasizes hands-on, experiential learning. 

I am still actively involved in international collaborations with institutions in the CGIAR. I contribute to projects that address sustainable agriculture and agroecology around the world. These collaborations have led to a number of high-impact publications and have enhanced the international visibility of both my research group and the University of Bonn. My involvement in these networks strengthens the global reach of our research, particularly in applying decision analysis to real-world environmental and agricultural challenges.

This thesis reflects the evolution of my scholarly work, integrating interdisciplinary approaches to advance agroecology, sustainable development, and decision analytical methods. The studies presented here were designed in collaboration with colleagues, graduate students, and research partners. My contributions include conceptualization, analysis, and manuscript preparation, as detailed in the next section.

For first-author papers [@whitney_decision_2023; @whitney_probabilistic_2018; @whitney_balancing_2025], I led the conceptualization, design, and execution of research. In co-authored works, I contributed methodological insights, data analysis, and writing. Many papers resulted from collaborations with graduate students, demonstrating my commitment to integrative and supportive research practices. Together the whole collection of work underscores my dedication to actionable science for addressing global challenges in agroecology and sustainable development. 

Throughout my career, I have navigated a diverse and interdisciplinary path, engaging with academia, government, and international organizations. These varied experiences have deepened my understanding of sustainable development, agroecology, and decision theory, shaping my approach to research. Working across different sectors and geographic contexts has strengthened my ability to lead complex, transdisciplinary projects, integrating diverse perspectives to address global challenges. As I move forward, I am committed to applying these insights to further scientific support for sustainable development.
